turn_text: Thank you for having me today. For many of us, the images coming out of Ukraine are not unfamiliar. They strike a deeply resonant chord in our stories and in our stories of our families. In 1919, nearly 100,000 Jews were murdered in the pogroms in Ukraine and Poland. And of course, decades later, many, many more would perish in the showa. By great grandparents, like so many families fleeing today, escaped the pogroms in Ukraine to save their lives. Once they made it to the United States, their son, my grandfather, chose to give back to the country that gave him so much. He tried to join the Marine Corps in 1942 and his mom dragged him out by his ear from the recruiting station. He snuck back in the next day. And in 1942, the Marine Corps was losing the war in the South Pacific, needed all the help they could get every rifle counted. Jews were being killed throughout the world and then Europe. And yet despite this, the Marine Corps sent him a 17-year-old skinny Jewish kid with no money to Purdue to study biomedical engineering, because they thought he was smart, changed his life. He became a pioneer in artificial limbs, and I think often of that story. In one of the lowest moments of World War II and one of the lowest moments of the Jewish people, the US government sent a Jewish kid to the Marine Corps and to school. They didn't give him anything, but they gave him a chance and he seized it. In that same spirit, we have a duty to not only welcome refugees from Ukraine when they come, But we also have a duty to protect the stranger overseas. And I know that this congregation in particular has done much for decades now for the people of Neapro, and will continue to do much for the people of Ukraine and their trials ahead. Protecting the stranger is a cornerstone of our faith, and I am committed to doing so at home and abroad. In our defense of democracy in Ukraine, we have a chance to restore our moral standing. President Putin justified his invasion on claims of denazification. That Vladimir Zelensky is a Jewish world leader with a biography rooted in the Shoah, and that Ukraine is home to one of the world's largest Jewish populations, a vibrant community that deserves a freedom to practice their faith, is a cruel, cruel irony of this unjustified and unprovoked invasion. Defending Ukraine means going further in terms of the actions that we're taking. So I want to take this opportunity to share with you how I'm thinking about this situation in Congress. And I'm looking forward to hearing your thoughts as we meet afterwards, because I'm going to stay to discuss this. I recently released a series of proposals that I hope will guide the conversation in Congress and with the administration about how we proceed in Ukraine. To start with, We have made significant progress in defending the free world. The current ban on oil imports is an important step for the United States. And the coordinated comprehensive sanctions from our NATO allies, and indeed from our allies throughout the world, has cratered the ruble. It has isolated the Russian economy. And it is depleting President Putin's moral standing at home while his military is bogged down in Ukraine. And yet it's not enough. To start, if America alone bans oil without support from our global actions, it's insufficient. America imports a very small percentage of Russia's exports, which are roughly five to six million barrels per day. Through diplomatic efforts, it is imperative that we coordinate a global embargo on Russian oil. This maneuver puts greater pressure on European nations should it include natural gas. But we can offer them support by maximizing our existing domestic and OPEC production to supply those in need. And indeed the administration is further pursuing innovative ideas as including exporting heat pumps to the European nations who are trying to wean themselves off Russian gas in the next several years. These heat pumps can go a long way in helping Europe with energy prices in the coming year. Aside from oil and gas, our diplomatic efforts must continue. The swift global condemnation of Russia's invasion was impressive. But China's initial silence was deafening, and now they are moving towards more overt support for Russian propaganda. With Russia's economy crippled by sanctions, presumably the Kremlin is going to turn to Beijing for help repeatedly. To circumvent this reaction, we should increase diplomatic pressure on Beijing to distance itself from the Kremlin, while considering secondary sanctions on Sino-Russian financial and commodities ties. China, for example, previously signed more than a $20 billion pledge to import Russian energy and food, and that contract needs to come under pressure. In Ukraine itself, with the battle waging on the ground, we must supply military and lethal aid. In partnership with our NATO allies, we should increase the supply of airplanes, drones, anti-tank, anti-aircraft, and anti-drown weapons to Ukrainian forces, while providing them with training. If necessary, through training camps in either Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, or Romania, any of the nations that border Ukraine. The Ukrainian forces are a fraction of the size of the Russian military, and we must provide them the assistance needed to defend their homeland. Now, importantly, at this point, that should not include a no-fly zone over Ukraine. I know that has come under significant conversation in recent weeks. It's important to remember that a no-fly zone is an active war, because a no-fly zone implies that we assert air supremacy over the Ukrainian airspace, and that means not just air-to-air combat from NATO fighter jets against Russian fighter jets who are currently contesting the skies with Ukrainian forces, but also air to surface strikes to disable Russian anti-aircraft technology, both in Eastern and Western Ukraine. That's direct war between the United States and another nuclear power, and that measure needs to be taken in consultation with Congress. And at this point, at this juncture, I think would be an escalation that is unnecessary and deeply dangerous. The Russian propaganda machine is feeding Russians and importantly Russian soldiers with lies. These Russian soldiers may think they are headed to Ukraine to wage a war against fascism to de-notify Ukraine, but upon arrival they realized the degree to which they were misled. This road map for a failed insurgency is not new to Russia in the 80s when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. The Soviet troops were similarly misguided. They entered Afghanistan with false assumptions and left defeated and demoralized. To spur demoralization against Russian troops in Ukraine, we must expand information operations. Through this, we will weaken Russian forces while increasing support for the Ukrainian resistance. Information operations can be as simple as mass text messages to Russian conscripts in Ukraine, explaining the state of affairs and the lack of logistical support for them, the lack of support. in the Russian homeland for what they are doing and the likelihood of their capture. But it can also extend into the Russian homeland itself, and in particular to the families of the Russian national security elite who are, at this point, Vladimir Putin's most important source of power and credibility in the Kremlin. While supporting Ukrainian resistance, we need also to work through legal and diplomatic channels to increase pressure on Russia. With Russian troops advancing across Ukraine, Orca setting a plan with Ukraine, Poland, Hungary, Romania, or Slovakia to host Ukrainian training facilities and a government in exile if remaining in Ukraine becomes untenable is crucial. Many of us will have heard the famous at this point line from President Vladimir Zelensky that he didn't need a ride, he needs ammunition, and while we can all support that bravado, The stark truth is, at this point, the most likely scenario still remains that Kiev will fall. The Russian military has proved itself to be incompetent, logistically poorly supplied, and with degraded command and control. It's still massively bigger than the Ukrainian forces, and with the indiscriminate shelling that they have taken on to cities, and with the importance that Kiev holds in Vladimir Putin's mind, we do need to prepare for the idea that Kiev might fall. And we need a government in exile. We need a government in exile partly because we need the international legal standing to continue to be able to provide lethal aid to the Ukrainian forces. Without a government in exile, it would be considered a breach of international law to be supporting a resistance against the sovereign nation. So whether that's in Lviv or in Poland or Romania or elsewhere, we've got to start planning for where the Ukrainian government might exercise its writ. Hopefully that doesn't happen, and Ukrainian resistance is much stronger than Russia anticipated. They were clearly relying on falsely rosy assumptions about Ukrainian will and about their own military competence. And so Russian forces are turning to depraved measures to harm Ukraine. Civilians are being targeted and killed. We all saw the news about the maternity ward that was shelled. They are now shelling libraries and museums and indiscriminately hitting apartment buildings as well. Partly, this is just depravity. And partly, this is a lack of military competence. What many experts expected was going to happen was that Russian infantry and special forces were going to be able to wage much more block by block surgical operations in the Russian-Ukrainian cities. They haven't been able to do that. They literally are unable to supply themselves with that kind of infantry maneuver, and so they're relying on tanks and artillery, which are indiscriminate in their shelling. And so they really don't, they're not able to target their objectives nearly as well as I thought they were gonna be able to be. And they don't have the boots on the ground that would allow them to be more precise in their targeting. So you combine that sort of blunt force military option that they have with Putin's lack of any respect for human life. And we have a situation that is really quite precarious for humanitarian protections. We cannot let Russia get away with these acts of barbarity. All Ukrainian forces, whether organized or guerrilla, should be recognized as combatants by the Kremlin, and the United States needs to insist on that. And we will make clear, as we have already, that atrocities against civilians will lead to prosecution against the Kremlin security elite, including President Putin at the Hague. And Ukraine has already filed several complaints to the International Criminal Court. As we keep that pressure up, We also must be sure that we're trying to dial the temperature down as we get into this saber rattling contest and indeed near direct military confrontation with another nuclear power. The United States must work with NATO to establish clear boundaries with Russia. NATO should issue a statement clarifying the actions that would trigger Article 5, the mutual defense portion of the NATO treaty, so that we avoid inadvertent escalation. So for example, if we're supplying aircraft, anti-aircraft, counter drone, drone equipment over the Ukrainian border from Poland or Romania, and the Russians are attacking those supplies as they're coming across the border, and some of those shells inadvertently go across the border into a NATO country. Does that count as an attack? We don't want to be figuring out that gray area after it happens when everybody is looking to rally around the flag. We want to figure out those gray areas ahead of time. The administration has established a direct communication hotline with the Kremlin, with Vladimir Putin himself from President Biden so that we can de-escalate those situations should they come up. But we need to also have clarity from NATO collectively about what actually would trigger an Article 5 escalation. Because while we stand by, That article, with every ounce of resolve, we also want to avoid inadvertent escalation that can lead to war unnecessarily. Similarly, parameters around cyber warfare need to be defined. There has been some surprise from security experts that Russia has not done more in cyber attacks. We can't expect that to continue. The United States, for its part, should wage deniable surgical cyber attacks on Russian command and control and logistics nodes within Ukraine. But while we do that, the Kremlin must also understand that NATO allies will not wage cyber attacks on the Russian homeland unless Russia cyber attacks and NATO nation first. Basically, we'll plausibly deny but wage surgical cyber attacks against logistics and C2 nodes within Ukraine. That's fair game. But we will make clear both publicly and through back channels that NATO should not and will not attack the Russian homeland. Any type of infrastructure with cyber attacks until unless Russia does so first against NATO nations. Russia has to this point demonstrated restraint. It is not waged any large-scale cyber attacks against NATO nations, and for so long as that continues, we will not do likewise against the Russian homeland. Ultimately, though, diplomatic efforts are the safest way to end this conflict. United States and its allies should present President Putin with an off-ramp for exiting Ukraine by indicating that NATO will still engage in security talks with him, and that progress towards a sovereign, secure, and democratic Ukraine will lead to calibrated sanctions relief. In recent weeks, we have seen a thread of chadon Freud, I think, in the coverage of the effects of sanctions against the Russian people. It has crippled their economy. It has created the ruble. It is leading to panic on the streets. And it is undermining President Putin standing at home. And yet we should remember that the point of what we are doing is not to hurt the Russian people. The point is to protect the sovereign, secure, and democratic Ukraine and to stand up for the international rule of law. and to protect the post-war American-led order. The famous Roman general Tacitus said that the best way to defeat an enemy was to box him in on three sides and to leave the fourth open so that he could escape without actually having to wage the fight. We have boxed in President Putin to this point on three sides. Between economic, diplomatic, and military setbacks, he is cornered. And yet, we need to be asking ourselves, as the sanctions' effects ratchet up, what's that fourth side that he can escape from? And we need to make clear, both publicly and through back channels, that we are going to work. And we will continue to work with Russia on legitimate security issues that it might have. But Ukraine is going to be sovereign, secure, and democratic. and that Russia's use of military might to try to remake the international order is absolutely unacceptable. It seems that Ukraine is signaling, and some intermediaries are signaling, that there could be a compromise in the works that recognizes the sovereignty and democracy in Ukraine, while yielding some suzerainty, I guess would be the technical word, to Russia over the Donbas, the small Donbas regions, not the larger regions that they've been defining it as, as well as Crimea. United States should continue to support talks in that vein. Whatever the final outcome is, it needs to be one that the Ukrainian president and NATO can support, and it needs to be one that is conducive to a sovereign, secure, and democratic Ukraine and for a lasting peace between them. Ukraine and the world are looking to America for guidance, and we must lead I think of the prayer for our country. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation. Neither shall they learn war anymore. For all of them, from the least to the greatest. From the least to the greatest shall know me. In these times of grave on settlement, peace can seem elusive. But that means our pursuit of peace is that much more essential. The proposals that I've outlined and that the Administration and Congress are working on are aiming for greater stability in Ukraine, and I will continue my own efforts to find a just and peaceable solution to welcome refugees, to defend democracy, and to restore America's standing as the leader of the free world. Thank you all for having me.
